phonemes.desc: Open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔ] with low tone, written with a dot below in standard Yoruba orthography.
Palatal approximant [j] followed by open [a] with high tone; the name means 'she tore'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'aw-YAH' — begin low in the chest on 'aw', then rise sharply to 'YAH'.

kin.label: Yoruba
kin.form: Ọya (also Òyá with tone marks), goddess of wind, storm, and transformation.

kin.label: Brazilian Candomblé
kin.form: Iansã, the whirlwind orixá of change and fire.

kin.label: Cuban Santería
kin.form: Oyá, syncretised with La Virgen de la Candelaria and Santa Teresa.

pronunciation.note: Ọya is Tier 1: the dot below marks a phonemic vowel distinction (open o versus close o) — a diacritic the ASCII form loses. Tonal variation, though crucial to Yoruba meaning, is not registrable in the DNS root zone.

domains.title: Lady of the Winds
domains.subtitle: Storms, Change, and the Cemetery Gate
domains.lead: Ọya is the orixá of wind, lightning, and radical change. She tears down what is finished so that something new can grow. In Yoruba cosmology she is the only female warrior to ride into battle alongside the thunder-god Ṣàngó, and she guards the threshold between the marketplace and the grave.

cards.name: Whirlwind
cards.desc: She arrives as a sudden gust that uproots trees and old assumptions.

cards.name: Warrior Queen
cards.desc: Wife of Ṣàngó and fearless general, she carries a sword and the irukere fly-whisk.

cards.name: Guardian of the Dead
cards.desc: She rules the cemetery gate and guides souls through transformation.

cards.name: Marketplace
cards.desc: Crossroads and markets are her terrain, where chance and commerce meet change.

symbols.name: Irukere (fly-whisk)
symbols.meaning: Her emblem of authority, used to summon and direct the winds.

symbols.name: Sword or machete
symbols.meaning: The blade that cuts away the obsolete and defends the community.

symbols.name: Buffalo horns
symbols.meaning: Her connection to the buffalo, symbol of ferocity and maternal power.

symbols.name: Nine colours
symbols.meaning: Her necklaces and cloth are often nine-coloured, especially burgundy and brown.

mythology.lead: Ọya's stories are told in Ifá divination, Candomblé praise-songs, and the oral traditions of the Yoruba and their diaspora. She is change embodied, and her myths turn on thresholds.

myths.title: Ọya and Ṣàngó
myths.text: Ọya was once married to the thunder-god Ṣàngó, or in some accounts she was his favourite companion in war. She learned the secrets of fire and lightning from him, but she is not his subordinate. When Ṣàngó fled in disgrace, Ọya tore apart the cloth of the sky with her winds, and some say she threw herself into the river that bears her name.

myths.title: The Niger and the Winds
myths.text: Ọya is the goddess of the Niger River (Odò-Ọya). She raises the winds that churn its surface and the storms that announce the rainy season. Fishermen and traders invoke her when they must cross her waters, for she can overturn a boat as easily as she can speed it home.

myths.title: She Who Tore
myths.text: Her very name means 'she tore'. In myth she tears the fabric of ordinary life to let the sacred through. To be possessed by Ọya in ritual is to be unmade and remade, to dance the destruction that clears the field for new growth. Those who fear her are usually those who cling too long to what is dying.

lore.syncretism: In the Afro-Atlantic religions, Ọya became Iansã in Brazilian Candomblé and Oyá in Cuban Santería, syncretised with Catholic saints associated with fire and protection. She is also linked to the spirits of the dead in New Orleans Voodoo. Wherever Yoruba people were dispersed, Ọya travelled as the orixá of necessary upheaval, her winds crossing the Atlantic itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ọya remains one of the most honoured orixás in the African diaspora. She appears in literature, dance, and feminist theology as a figure of female power that is not domesticated. Her colours fly at Candomblé ceremonies; her winds are invoked at crossroads. In an age of climate change and social upheaval, Ọya speaks with uncomfortable relevance: the storm is not cruelty; it is the only way the forest can renew itself.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ọya is the goddess we pray to when we are afraid of what must end. She does not promise gentle transformation. Her winds tear roofs from houses and uproot trees that have stood for decades. Yet without her, the air would stagnate and the soil would never clear for new seed.

To sit with Ọya is to ask what in your life has completed its season. She does not answer with comfort. She answers with a gust that slams the door and a flash of lightning that shows, for one instant, exactly what must go. Her gift is not the storm itself; it is the cleared ground that remains after it passes.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is Yoruba: Ọya. Yoruba is a tonal language; the standard written form uses a dot below ọ to distinguish open [ɔ] from close [o]. The full tonal spelling is Òyá (low tone, then high tone), but tone marks are not registrable in the DNS root zone. The meaning 'she tore' derives from the verb yà. PUNICODEX therefore registers Ọya with the dot below, preserving the distinctive open vowel.
